2. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
On 17-06-2019 at about 8.15 a.m., the deceased petitioner by name A. Raghavaiah @
Annamaneni Raghavaiah was crossing the Mahadevapura Ring road, infront of More Mega Store, carefully, cautiously, observing all the moving traffic.

At that time a Bullet motorcycle bearing Reg. No.KA- 21-W-5482, ridden by its rider at high speed,
in rash and negligent manner, without following any traffic rules and regulations, so as to endangering to human life and property, all of a sudden came and dashed against the petitioner.
Due to said impact, the deceased petitioner fell down and sustained grievous.

Immediately after the accident, he was shifted to Bowring and Lady Curzon Hospital, Bengaluru, wherein he took first aid treatment and then he was shifted to NIMHANS Hospital and then he was shifted to Sai Ambika Hospital,
wherein he took treatment as an in-patient and underwent surgery.

sentences.text: After undergoing treatment, the deceased petitioner died due to the accidental injuries.
Earlier to the accident, the deceased was running P.G. Centre and was earning Rs.25,000/- per month.
He was contributing his entire earnings to his family.
Due to untimely death of a sole bread earner, the petitioners are struggling for their livelihood.

The K.R.
Puram Traffic Police have registered the case against the rider of the said motorcycle for the offences punishable under Section 279 and 337 of I.P.C. The respondent No.1 is the owner and respondent No.2 is the insurer of the offending vehicle.
Hence, they are jointly and severally liable to pay compensation to the petitioners.
Therefore, it is prayed to allow the petition and award compensation of Rs.20,00,000/- with interest at the rate of 12% per annum.
3. On service of notice to the respondents, the respondents No.1 and 2 have appeared through their counsel.
The respondent No.2 has filed its written statement.
Whereas, the respondent No.1 did not choose to file his written statement.
4. The respondent No.2 in its written statement has denied all the allegations made in the petition.
It has admitted the issuance of insurance policy in favour of respondent No.1, in respect of the motorcycle bearing No.KA- 21-W-5482 and its validity as on the date of accident.
It has contended that, the rider of the offending vehicle was not holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the same as on the date of accident.
It seeks protection under Section 147 and 149 of Motor Vehicles Act.
It has contended that, the petition is bad for non compliance of provision under Sections 134(c) and 158(6) of Motor Vehicles Act.
It has denied the age, avocation and income of the petitioner/deceased, injuries, medical expenses and treatment taken by him.

It has contended that,
the insured vehicle is not at all involved in any accident and it was intentionally implicated in collusion with the owner, rider and other authorities in order to get the unlawful benefit from the insurance company.
Further it is contended that, immediately after the accident no complaint is lodged before the police and there was an inordinate delay in lodging the complaint.
Further, it has sought permission to contest even on behalf of respondent No.1 under Section 170 of the Motor Vehicles Act.

Further it is contended that, the compensation claimed is highly excessive and Raghavaiah Alias Annamaneni ... vs Siju K.A on 9 April, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69255150/

11. On meticulously going through the police documents marked as Ex.P.1 to 7, it clearly reveals that,
the accident in question has occurred due to rash and negligent riding of the rider of offending motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W-5482 and dashing the same to the deceased petitioner who was crossing the road.
Further it reveals that, the deceased petitioner has sustained grievous injury on his left leg in the said accident.

The investigation officer in his final report/charge-sheet, which is marked as Ex.P.7, has clearly stated that, the accident has taken place due to rash and negligent riding of the rider of offending motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W-5482.
12.

At the outset, it is pertinent to note that, the date, time and place of accident, issuance of insurance policy by the respondent No.2 in respect of offending motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W-5482 and its validity as on the date of accident, are not in dispute.
Further, the above oral and documentary evidence placed on record by the petitioner has remained undisputed by the respondent No.1, who is owner of offending vehicle bearing Reg. No. KA-21-W-5482.

Whereas, the respondent No.2 insurance company has specifically denied the above averred facts and circumstances of the accident and taken specific defence that, the accident has taken place due to sole negligence of the deceased petitioner, the offending motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W- 5482 is not at all involved in the alleged accident and the deceased petitioner in collusion with the owner of said vehicle and the police has falsely implicated the said vehicle in the alleged accident, in order to have wrongful gain from the insurance company and the rider of the offending vehicle was not holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the same as on the date of accident.
But, the respondent No.2 has failed to establish the said contentions.

Except the self serving statements of R.W.1, there is absolutely no other oral or documentary evidence placed on record by the respondent No.2 to show that, the accident has occurred due to sole negligence of the deceased petitioner and the offending motorcycle bearing Reg. No.KA- 21-W-5482 was not at all involved in the alleged accident.

On the other hand, the oral and documentary evidence placed on record by the petitioners clearly establishes that, the accident in question has taken place due to rash and negligent riding of the rider of motorcycle bearing Reg. No.KA-21-W-5482 and dashing the same to the deceased petitioner who was crossing the road.

Though, the learned counsel for respondent No.2 has cross-examined P.W.1 in length, nothing worth has been elicited from his mouth which creates doubt on the veracity of her evidence or which establishes that, the accident in question has occurred due sole negligence of the deceased petitioner or there was any contributory negligence on his part in the cause of accident.

Further, the P.W.1 has unequivocally denied the suggestion that,
the alleged accident has occurred due to sole negligence of the deceased petitioner and there was no fault on the part of the rider of motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W- 5482.
The oral evidence of P.W.1 is fully corroborated with the documentary evidence placed on record by the petitioner.

14. No doubt, there is a delay of one day in lodging the complaint in respect of accident in question,
by the grand- son of deceased petitioner.

It is settled proposition of law that, mere delay in lodging the complaint in a motor accident claim cases is not fatal, if adequate explanation for delay is offered and it should not be a ground to reject the claim petition.
It gains relevance in the cases where other evidence does not support the claimant's allegations.

In the present case, it is clearly stated in the Ex.P.2 first information statement/complaint that, immediately after the accident the deceased petitioner was shifted to NIMHANS Hospital and after scanning as per doctor's advise he was shifted to Sai Ambika Hospital.
Further, it is clearly stated in the Ex.P.1 F.I.R., that due to hospitalisation there is delay in lodging the complaint.
There is nothing on record to disbelieve the said version.

There is no rebuttal evidence placed on record by the respondent No.2 to show that,
the reason for delay stated in the Ex.P.1 & 2 is false and even nothing with respect to same has been elicited in the cross-examination of P.W.1.

In such circumstances, there is no impediment to believe the reasons for delay stated in Ex.P.1 first information report and Ex.P.2 complaint and hold that,
the delay caused in lodging the complaint in the present case has been properly and adequately explained.

15. Further, the Ex.P.6 wound certificate and Ex.P.8 discharge summary, clearly speaks that, the deceased petitioner had sustained grievous injuries i.e. right frontal SDH and left both bone fracture.

Further, the Ex.P.8 discharge summary issued by Sai Ambica Hospital, Bengaluru, clearly speaks that, on 17-06-2019 the injured Raghavaiah was brought to the hospital with history injuries to left leg, chest and forehead and he has been treated in the said hospital as an in-patient from 17-06-2019 to 22-06- 2019.

Further it reveals that, the deceased petitioner has undergone surgery for the said injuries i.e. ORIF with IMIL nail and wound debridement of left leg done under GA and he was discharged with an advise for follow up treatment.

On the other hand, the respondent No.2 insurance company though has denied the authenticity of said documents, has not produced any rebuttal evidence to show that, the deceased petitioner has not sustained the above said injuries and the medical records produced by the petitioners are false.

Therefore, in such circumstances, there is no impediment to believe the final report filed by the investigation officer and other police records,
regarding the place, date and time of accident, involvement of the offending motorcycle bearing Reg.

16. It is well settled principle of law that, in a case relating to the Motor Accident Claims, the claimants are not required to prove the case as required to be done in a criminal trial.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in the case of Parameshwari V/s Amir Chand and others, reported in (2011) SCC 635, has clearly held that, "in a road accident claim cases the strict principle of proof as in a criminal case are not required."

But,

After lapse of 3 years from the date of discharge from the hospital, Raghavaiah @
Annamaneni Raghavaiah has died.
As per Ex.P.12 death certificate he has died on 25-07-2022.

There is absolutely no material on record to show that, after discharge from the Sai Ambica Hospital till the date of his death Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah was under follow up treatment for the injuries sustained in the accident and he has died to the said injuries.
There is no nexus between the injuries sustained by Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah in the accident and cause of his death.

The petitioners have neither examined any doctor, nor they have produced any document to show that, deceased Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah has died due to the injuries sustained in the accident in question.
Even, there is no post- mortem report produced by the petitioner in the case to establish the cause of his death.

In such circumstances, there is no other option before this Court except to hold that, the deceased Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah has not died due to injuries sustained in the accident in question.

23. Liability:
Admittedly, as on the date of accident the respondent No.2 is the insurer and respondent No.1 is the owner of the offending vehicle.

Further, the evidence placed on record by the petitioner clearly establishes that, due to rash and negligent riding of the rider of offending vehicle bearing Reg. No. KA-21-W-5482 the said accident has occurred.
In such circumstances, the respondent No.1 being the owner of said vehicle is vicariously liable to compensate for the damages caused by the said vehicle.

The respondent No.2 being the insurer of the vehicle has to indemnify the respondent No.1.
24.

But, the respondent No.2 insurance company has taken specific contentions in its written statement that, as on the date of accident the respondent No.1/rider of the offending vehicle was not holding valid and effective driving licence to drive the said motorcycle.
As there is breach of conditions of the policy, the respondent No.2 insurance company is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1.

In such circumstances, the burden was on the respondent No.1 to prove that, at the of accident he was holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the offending motorcycle bearing No. KA-21-W-5482.

But, the respondent No.1 has failed to discharge his burden in the case,
as he did not choose to contest the case of the petitioner by filing his written statement.

25. The learned counsel for respondent No.2 insurance company vehemently argued that, the Ex.P.1 Insurance Policy clearly speaks that, the policy covers the risk provided the driver of insured vehicle holds valid and effective driving licence at the time of accident and he is not disqualified from holding or obtaining such a licence.
The respondent No.1 has not produced any document to show that, as on the date of accident his was holding valid & effective driving licence to ride the offending motorcycle.
Even, no document has been produced by the petitioners with respect to same.

The Ex.P.7 charge-sheet clearly speaks that, as on the date of accident the accused/rider of the offending motorcycle bearing Reg. No. KA-21-W-5482 was not holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the said motorcycle and hence in addition to the offence punishable under Sec.279 and 338 of I.P.C., he has been charge-sheeted for offence punishable U/Sec.3(1) R/w 181 of Motor Vehicles Act.
Further argued that, the final report filed by the investigation officer has not been challenged by the respondent No.1.

26. On the other hand, the learned counsel for petitioner vehemently argued that, it is settled principle of law that, even if there is a fundamental breach of any condition recognised under Sec.149(2) of Motor vehicles Act, the insurance company is liable to pay the third party and recover from the insured.
27.

As rightly argued by the learned counsel for the respondent No.2, as per the Ex.P.7 final report/charge-sheet, at the time accident the accused/respondent No.1/rider of offending motorcycle bearing No. KA-21-W-5482 was not holding driving licence to drive the said vehicle and hence in addition to the offence punishable under Sec.279 and 338 of I.P.C., he has been charge-sheeted for offence punishable U/Sec.3(1) R/w 181 of Motor Vehicles Act and admittedly, the said final report/charge-sheet has not been challenged by the respondent No.1.

In such circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that, the respondent No.1 cannot be permitted to take the benefit of his wrong and the respondent No.2/Insurance Company is entitled to raise a defence under Sec.149(2) of Motor Vehicles Act.

Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that, as there is breach of fundamental condition of the Ex.R.1 insurance policy by the insured/respondent No.1, the respondent No.2 insurance company is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.2.

Accordingly, holding that the respondent No.1 being the owner of offending vehicle is liable to pay the above compensation amount Rs.1,86,425/- to the petitioner, with interest at the rate of 6% per annum from the date of petition till its realization, I answer Issue No.2 in Partly Affirmative.
28. Issue No.3:
In view of the above findings, I proceed to pass the following order:
ORDER The petition is partly allowed with costs.

The petitioners No.1(a) to (d) are entitled to compensation of Rs.1,86,425/- (Rupees one lakh eighty six thousand four hundred and twenty five only) with interest at the rate of 6% p.a., from the date of petition till realisation.
The respondent No.1 is liable to pay the above compensation amount to the petitioners and he is directed to pay the same within two months from the date of this order.
The above compensation amount shall be apportioned equally among the petitioner No.1(a) to 1(d).

The entire compensation amount with proportionate interest awarded in favour of petitioner No.1(a) to (d) shall be released in their favour through e- payment on proper identification and verification.

ISSUES

2. Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation?
If so, what is the quantum and from whom ?

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
Whereas, the respondent No.2 insurance company has specifically denied the above averred facts and circumstances of the accident and taken specific defence that, the accident has taken place due to sole negligence of the deceased petitioner, the offending motorcycle bearing No.KA-21-W- 5482 is not at all involved in the alleged accident and the deceased petitioner in collusion with the owner of said vehicle and the police has falsely implicated the said vehicle in the alleged accident, in order to have wrongful gain from the insurance company and the rider of the offending vehicle was not holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the same as on the date of accident.
Except the self serving statements of R.W.1, there is absolutely no other oral or documentary evidence placed on record by the respondent No.2 to show that, the accident has occurred due to sole negligence of the deceased petitioner and the offending motorcycle bearing Reg. No.KA- 21-W-5482 was not at all involved in the alleged accident.
When the accident was not occurred due to the any mechanical defects in the offending vehicle and there was no negligence on the part of the deceased petitioner, then it can be presumed that, the said accident had occurred due to rash and negligent riding of the rider of offending vehicle.
If really as contended by the respondent No.2, if the said vehicle was not at all involved in the accident, the immediate question that arises is, how the front portion parts of the said motorcycle got damaged.
It is not the case of the respondent No.2 that, the said damage were already existing before the accident in question or the same were caused in some other accident.
14. No doubt, there is a delay of one day in lodging the complaint in respect of accident in question,
by the grand- son of deceased petitioner.
It is settled proposition of law that, mere delay in lodging the complaint in a motor accident claim cases is not fatal, if adequate explanation for delay is offered and it should not be a ground to reject the claim petition.
It gains relevance in the cases where other evidence does not support the claimant's allegations.
Therefore, in such circumstances, there is no impediment to believe the final report filed by the investigation officer and other police records,
regarding the place, date and time of accident, involvement of the offending motorcycle bearing Reg.

6 No. KA-21-W-5482 in the accident, rash and negligent riding of the rider of offending motorcycle and the injuries caused to deceased Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah in the said accident.
16. It is well settled principle of law that, in a case relating to the Motor Accident Claims, the claimants are not required to prove the case as required to be done in a criminal trial.
After lapse of 3 years from the date of discharge from the hospital, Raghavaiah @
Annamaneni Raghavaiah has died.
As per Ex.P.12 death certificate he has died on 25-07-2022.
There is absolutely no material on record to show that, after discharge from the Sai Ambica Hospital till the date of his death Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah was under follow up treatment for the injuries sustained in the accident and he has died to the said injuries.
There is no nexus between the injuries sustained by Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah in the accident and cause of his death.
The petitioners have neither examined any doctor, nor they have produced any document to show that, deceased Raghavaiah @ Annamaneni Raghavaiah has died due to the injuries sustained in the accident in question.
Even, there is no post- mortem report produced by the petitioner in the case to establish the cause of his death.
The respondent No.2 being the insurer of the vehicle has to indemnify the respondent No.1.
24.
As there is breach of conditions of the policy, the respondent No.2 insurance company is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.1.
In such circumstances, the burden was on the respondent No.1 to prove that, at the of accident he was holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the offending motorcycle bearing No. KA-21-W-5482.
But, the respondent No.1 has failed to discharge his burden in the case,
as he did not choose to contest the case of the petitioner by filing his written statement.
The respondent No.1 has not produced any document to show that, as on the date of accident his was holding valid & effective driving licence to ride the offending motorcycle.
The Ex.P.7 charge-sheet clearly speaks that, as on the date of accident the accused/rider of the offending motorcycle bearing Reg. No. KA-21-W-5482 was not holding valid and effective driving licence to ride the said motorcycle and hence in addition to the offence punishable under Sec.279 and 338 of I.P.C., he has been charge-sheeted for offence punishable U/Sec.3(1) R/w 181 of Motor Vehicles Act.
In such circumstances, this Court is of the opinion that, the respondent No.1 cannot be permitted to take the benefit of his wrong and the respondent No.2/Insurance Company is entitled to raise a defence under Sec.149(2) of Motor Vehicles Act.
Therefore, this Court is of the considered opinion that, as there is breach of fundamental condition of the Ex.R.1 insurance policy by the insured/respondent No.1, the respondent No.2 insurance company is not liable to indemnify the respondent No.2.
